passage:
Tuesday, late. Ma's scan results come on Thursday and I have been pacing the flat since six. So I took the back of an envelope and made two lists. Things I can do: book the driver for Thursday, ask the clinic what papers to carry, call my sister Farida so we share the waiting. Things I cannot do: decide what the report says. I read that last line twice, and my chest loosened, like a knot given a little slack. Then I caught myself opening the search page again, and I closed the laptop instead. Dinner was dal and rice, eaten sitting down, the first proper meal today. Whatever Thursday brings, I will not be carrying it alone.
Mohit

qa.q: What did Mohit write on the back of the envelope?
qa.a: Two lists: things Mohit can do, such as booking the driver for Thursday and calling Farida, and things Mohit cannot do, such as deciding what the report says.

qa.q: What did Mohit feel after reading the last line of the lists twice?
qa.a: A little relief. The chest loosened like a knot given slack, so the worry felt lighter even though the results were still to come.

qa.q: Which choice helped Mohit turn worry into something manageable?
qa.a: Mohit split the worry into tasks that were possible and stopped trying to control the report itself, then shared the waiting with Farida instead of holding it alone.

qa.q: How might Farida feel about being called?
qa.a: Farida may feel trusted and glad to share the waiting, since Mohit asked to split it rather than carry it alone.

grounding: A worried adult child does what is possible, releases what is not in their hands, and feels the worry ease.

passage:
Nitin: you still up? demo is at ten tomorrow
Parul: yes. rechecking slide 14 for the fifth time
Nitin: what's left on your side?
Parul: nothing really. everything's tested, backup is on the drive
Nitin: so what are you checking?
Parul: whether they'll like it. which I can't control 😅
Nitin: exactly. you did your part
Parul: hmm. true. it's the waiting part that's loud in my head
Nitin: then close the laptop and make tea
Parul: ok. closing it. tea 🙂
Nitin: send me a photo of the tea
Parul: deal. see you at 9:30

qa.q: What is Parul rechecking late at night?
qa.a: Slide 14, for the fifth time.

qa.q: What is Parul worried about, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Parul worries whether the audience will like the demo; the fifth recheck of a finished slide and the joke about it show the anxiety about something outside Parul's control.

qa.q: What could Parul do to stop the worry from taking over the evening?
qa.a: Parul could do what Nitin suggested: accept that the tested work is done, close the laptop and make tea, leaving the audience's reaction alone.

qa.q: How might Nitin see Parul's late-night rechecking?
qa.a: As an understandable worry about something outside Parul's control, which is why Nitin asks what is left, says Parul did the part that is Parul's, and jokes about the tea photo.

grounding: A person worried about a project's outcome sees they have done their part and releases the rest.

passage: Tarun's father had been in the district hospital in Satara for four days, and Tarun, twenty-five, was running between the ward and their village forty minutes away. He couldn't sleep. He kept checking his phone for bad news. On the fifth morning, Farida, who ran the medical shop near the bus stand, found him staring at the ceiling fan. "Write two lists," she said, handing him a receipt pad. He did. In my hands: bring clean clothes, ask the doctor my questions at the evening round, keep the cows fed, eat something, sleep. Not in my hands: how fast Baba heals, what the tests show. He stared at the second list for a long time. Then he folded it and put it in his pocket. That night he fed the cows, ate two rotis, and slept for six hours without checking his phone once.

qa.q: How far was the hospital from Tarun's village?
qa.a: Forty minutes away.

qa.q: How did Tarun feel before Farida handed him the pad?
qa.a: He was anxious and exhausted, unable to sleep and constantly checking his phone for bad news.

qa.q: Why did Farida's two lists help Tarun?
qa.a: They separated what he could do from what he couldn't, so he could act on the first list and set down the worry about the second.

qa.q: How might Tarun's father benefit from Tarun letting go of control?
qa.a: He would have a son who is rested and clear when asking the doctor questions at the evening round, instead of one worn out by worry.

grounding: Shows a young adult worried about his father's health doing what he can and releasing the rest, which eases his suffering.

passage: Daniel had spent eight months on the grant application for his community-garden project in Porto. On Friday he clicked submit at 4:58 pm, two minutes before the deadline. The decision would take six weeks. That weekend he refreshed his email forty times. On Sunday, Beatriz found him rereading the budget table. "Did you do everything you could?" she asked. He thought. "I checked every number. I asked three people to review it. I got the letters of support." "Then what's left?" "Waiting." "And is waiting yours to do anything about?" He laughed, a bit tired. "No." Beatriz tossed him his swimming bag. "Then let's go to the sea." At the beach he still thought about the grant, but he didn't refresh anything. For six weeks he worked on the garden with the kids, grant or no grant.

qa.q: How long would the grant decision take?
qa.a: Six weeks.

qa.q: How did Daniel feel during the weekend after submitting?
qa.a: He was anxious and restless, refreshing his email forty times and rereading the budget table.

qa.q: What small step did Beatriz suggest, and why did it help?
qa.a: She asked what was still his to do, then took him to the sea, helping him release the waiting he couldn't control.

qa.q: How might the kids at the garden benefit from Daniel letting go?
qa.a: They got his full attention on the garden for six weeks, instead of a distracted Daniel checking email.

grounding: Shows a young adult who did everything possible for a project's outcome and then released what was out of his hands.

passage: In the surgery waiting room of the city hospital in Kolkata, Samir couldn't sit still. His mother had gone in at nine. It was now eleven thirty. He paced, checked the board, asked the nurse twice. His sister Swati pulled him onto the bench. "Samir. What can we actually do right now?" He opened his mouth to say "nothing" and stopped. "We can call Mama and tell him. We can eat something. We can make sure the forms are signed." "And what can't we do?" He swallowed. "The surgery." "So let's do our list." Samir called Mama. Swati got two cups of tea and a packet of biscuits. They signed the last form at the desk. When they sat down again, Samir didn't pace. He still watched the doors, but his hands were still. At one fifteen, the doctor came out smiling.

qa.q: What time had their mother gone in for surgery?
qa.a: At nine.

qa.q: What was Samir feeling as he paced and checked the board?
qa.a: Samir was anxious and restless, unable to sit still while waiting.

qa.q: Which part of Swati's approach helped most, and why?
qa.a: Asking what they could actually do turned helpless waiting into a short list of actions, which calmed Samir.

qa.q: How might Swati have been feeling while helping her brother?
qa.a: She was probably worried too, but steadier, and chose to help them both through the wait.

grounding: Shows a young adult waiting during a parent's surgery separating what is in his hands from what is not, which reduces his suffering.

passage:
Nirmala,
Thank you for the call last night. You asked how I'm coping with Papa's surgery on Thursday, and I didn't have a real answer then. Here's what I've worked out since.
Things in my hands: I've booked the Wednesday night bus. I've spoken to the doctor's assistant and written down every question Ma wanted to ask. I've sorted out leave with my manager. I'll sit with Papa before they take him in.
Things not in my hands: how the surgery goes, how fast he heals, whether the ward is noisy.
For two weeks I've been checking my phone at 3 am as if worrying were my job. Tonight I wrote both lists on one page and put the second list in my drawer. I'm still scared. But I slept six hours.
Jyoti

qa.q: When is Papa's surgery?
qa.a: It is on Thursday.

qa.q: How was Jyoti feeling in the two weeks before writing the lists?
qa.a: Jyoti felt anxious and restless, checking the phone at 3 am as if worrying were a job.

qa.q: Why did splitting the worries into two lists help?
qa.a: It let Jyoti put full effort into what could be done and set down what could not, so the fear stayed but sleep came back.

qa.q: How might Ma feel knowing Jyoti wrote down her questions?
qa.a: Ma may feel supported and less alone, knowing her worries will be asked about properly.

grounding: Shows a young adult worried about a parent's surgery doing what is possible and releasing what is outside their hands.
